title: Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Current

toc.title: 16.1 Faraday's and Lenz's laws; the AC generator, the transformer and eddy currents
16.2 Self and mutual inductance; energy stored in an inductor
16.3 Peak and rms values; impedance, phase, power and Q-factor of LCR circuits

html:
This chapter is where a changing magnetic field becomes a voltage. The area Current Electricity and Magnetism carries 9 of the 50 Physics questions (official MEC weightage), and we estimate 3 come from here.

The paper asks for Faraday's law in one-line form, the direction of an induced current, the peak emf of a generator, a transformer ratio, the rms value, an impedance or resonance calculation, and the shape of a rectified waveform.

The marks are lost on three things: rms against peak in a power calculation, a transformer claimed to work on DC, and the direction of Lenz's law.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • \Phi=BA\cos\theta; \varepsilon=-N\,d\Phi/dt; average emf N\Delta\Phi/\Delta t; motional emf \varepsilon=Bvl.
  • Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change that produced it — energy conservation, not a arbitrary rule about poles.
  • The force needed to keep a rod moving, F=B^2l^2v/R, and the power Fv=\varepsilon^2/R.
  • Generator: \varepsilon=NBA\omega\sin\omega t, peak \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega; the transformer: V_s/V_p=N_s/N_p=I_p/I_s, AC only, no change of frequency; eddy currents and lamination.
  • Self and mutual inductance, \varepsilon=-L\,dI/dt, L=\mu_0N^2A/l, U=\frac12LI^2.
  • rms =I_0/\sqrt{2}; X_L=\omega L, X_C=1/\omega C; Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}; resonance at f_0=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}); P=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi; Q=\omega_0L/R.
  • The bridge rectifier: four diodes, both half-cycles, ripple frequency 2f.

16.1 Faraday's and Lenz's laws; the AC generator, the transformer and eddy currents

16.1.1 Magnetic flux and flux linkage

The magnetic flux through a surface is the number of field lines crossing it:

\Phi=BA\cos\theta

where A is the area, B the flux density and \theta the angle between \vec B and the normal to the surface. The unit is the weber (Wb): 1 Wb = 1 T m².

For a coil of N turns, each turn encloses the same flux, so the flux linkage is N\Phi. It is measured in weber-turns, numerically equal to Wb.

Situation \theta Flux
Surface perpendicular to \vec B 0° maximum, BA
Surface parallel to \vec B 90° zero
Coil rotated from perpendicular to parallel 0° → 90° falls from BA to 0

16.1.2 Faraday's law

Faraday's law of induction

The emf induced in a circuit equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux linkage through it:

\varepsilon=-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}

The average emf over a time interval is

\bar\varepsilon=-N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=-N\frac{\Phi_2-\Phi_1}{\Delta t}

The emf can be raised by more turns, a stronger field, a larger area, or a faster change. It is the rate of change that matters, not the flux itself: a coil sitting in a strong steady field has no induced emf at all.

The minus sign is Lenz's law, and it is not optional bookkeeping — it is the statement that the induced emf drives a current whose own field opposes the change.

16.1.3 Lenz's law and energy conservation

Lenz's law

The direction of the induced current is such that it opposes the change in flux that produced it.

Push the north pole of a bar magnet towards a coil. The flux through the coil increases towards the magnet, so the induced current makes the near face of the coil a north pole, which repels the approaching magnet.

Pull the magnet away and the flux decreases, so the near face becomes a south pole and attracts it. Either way the coil fights the motion.

That fight is where the energy comes from. You do mechanical work against the repulsion; the induced current dissipates that work as heat in the coil's resistance.

If the induced current instead helped the magnet, the magnet would accelerate for free and the circuit would deliver energy from nothing. Lenz's law is therefore the law of conservation of energy in disguise.

Change in flux Induced current Result
Flux into the coil increases Sets up a field out of the coil Opposes the increase
Flux into the coil decreases Sets up a field into the coil Opposes the decrease
Magnet approaches, N pole first Near face becomes N Repels the magnet
Magnet recedes, N pole first Near face becomes S Attracts the magnet
Lenz is about the change, not the flux

The induced current does not oppose the flux; it opposes the change in flux. A coil in a strong steady field has no induced current at all, and a coil in a weak field that is changing fast has a large one.

Questions that say "the flux is large, so the induced emf is large" are testing exactly this confusion.

16.1.4 Motional emf

A conducting rod of length l moves with speed v perpendicular to a uniform field B, on rails that form a closed circuit.

The free electrons in the rod move with it and feel a magnetic force qvB along the rod; charge separates until the electric field along the rod balances it, giving an emf

\varepsilon=Bvl

The same result comes from Faraday's law. In time dt the rod sweeps area lv\,dt, so the flux changes by Blv\,dt and \varepsilon=d\Phi/dt=Blv.

If the circuit has resistance R,

I=\frac{Bvl}{R}, \qquad F=BIl=\frac{B^2l^2v}{R}

The force is the magnetic drag on the rod, and it points opposite to the motion. To keep the rod moving at constant speed you must pull with this force, delivering mechanical power

P=Fv=\frac{B^2l^2v^2}{R}=\frac{\varepsilon^2}{R}

which is exactly the electrical power I^2R dissipated in the circuit. The mechanical work you do becomes heat — Lenz's law again, now in numbers.

Two powers, one answer

F=B^2l^2v/R grows as v^2 in the power, so doubling the speed of the rod needs four times the force? No — the force itself goes as v, and the power as v^2. Read the question: it may ask for the force, the power, or the current.

Worked example 16.1 — a rod on rails

Problem. A rod 0.50 m long moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a field of 0.20 T. The circuit resistance is 0.20 Ω. Find the emf, the current, the force needed to keep the rod moving, and the power dissipated.

Solution. \varepsilon=Bvl=(0.20)(4.0)(0.50)=0.40\ \text{V}.

I=\varepsilon/R=0.40/0.20=2.0\ \text{A}.

F=BIl=(0.20)(2.0)(0.50)=0.20\ \text{N}.

P=Fv=(0.20)(4.0)=0.80\ \text{W}, and I^2R=(2.0)^2(0.20)=0.80\ \text{W} ✓.

16.1.5 The AC generator

A rectangular coil of N turns and area A rotates with constant angular speed \omega in a uniform field B. The flux through it is

\Phi=NBA\cos\omega t

so the induced emf is

\varepsilon=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=NBA\omega\sin\omega t=\varepsilon_0\sin\omega t, \qquad \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega

Position of the coil Flux Rate of change emf
Plane perpendicular to \vec B maximum, NBA zero zero
Plane parallel to \vec B zero maximum maximum, \varepsilon_0
After a quarter turn from perpendicular zero maximum maximum

The emf is not maximum when the flux is maximum; it is maximum when the flux is changing fastest, which is when the flux is zero. The two are a quarter cycle apart.

The coil ends are joined to two slip rings with brushes, so the output is alternating. A split-ring commutator instead reverses the connections every half turn and gives direct current — that is the difference between an AC and a DC generator.

Worked example 16.2 — peak and average emf

Problem. A coil of 200 turns and area 0.020 m² rotates at 60 rad s⁻¹ in a field of 0.50 T. Find the peak emf and the emf when the plane of the coil is at 30° to the field.

Solution. \varepsilon_0=NBA\omega=(200)(0.50)(0.020)(60)=120\ \text{V}.

When the plane is at 30° to the field, the normal is at 60^{\circ} to it, so \omega t=60^{\circ} from the perpendicular position and \varepsilon=\varepsilon_0\sin60^{\circ}=120(0.866)=104\ \text{V}.

Watch the angle: \sin\omega t is measured from the position of maximum flux, where the plane is perpendicular to the field.

16.1.6 The transformer

A transformer has two coils wound on a common laminated soft-iron core. Alternating current in the primary sets up an alternating flux in the core; that flux links the secondary and induces an emf in it.

Because the same flux passes through each turn of both coils, the emf per turn is the same:

\frac{V_s}{V_p}=\frac{N_s}{N_p}

For an ideal transformer (no losses) the power in equals the power out, V_pI_p=V_sI_s, so

\frac{I_s}{I_p}=\frac{N_p}{N_s}

A step-up transformer has N_s>N_p: it raises the voltage and lowers the current. A step-down transformer has N_s<N_p: it lowers the voltage and raises the current.

Step-up Step-down
Turns N_s>N_p N_s<N_p
Voltage rises falls
Current falls rises
Power (ideal) unchanged unchanged
Example transmission line at 132 kV 220 V supply to a 12 V charger

Why it needs AC. The secondary emf depends on d\Phi/dt.

A direct current gives a steady flux, d\Phi/dt=0, and no secondary emf at all — the transformer simply does not work on DC, and connecting one to a DC supply can burn out the primary because there is no back emf to limit the current.

For the same reason a transformer cannot change the frequency: one cycle of the primary flux produces exactly one cycle of secondary emf.

Losses and remedies.

Loss Cause Remedy
Copper loss I^2R heating in the windings thick wire of low resistivity
Eddy-current loss currents induced in the solid core laminated core, thin insulated sheets
Hysteresis loss repeated magnetisation of the core soft iron core with a narrow loop
Flux leakage flux that misses the secondary wind the coils close together on the same core

Efficiency \eta=P_{out}/P_{in}\times100\,\%; a good large transformer reaches 98 %.

Transformer myths

A transformer does not change the frequency, does not work on steady DC, and does not create power.

It changes voltage and current in opposite directions, and the product VI stays (almost) the same. "A step-up transformer increases the power" is wrong in three separate ways.

Worked example 16.3 — transformer currents

Problem. A transformer has 1000 primary turns and 50 secondary turns. The primary is connected to 220 V and delivers 2.0 A. Find the secondary voltage and current, assuming an ideal transformer.

Solution. \dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}=\dfrac{50}{1000}=0.05, so V_s=0.05(220)=11\ \text{V}.

V_pI_p=220(2.0)=440\ \text{W}, so I_s=440/11=40\ \text{A}.

The voltage falls by 20 and the current rises by 20 — the power is unchanged.

16.1.7 Eddy currents

When a bulk piece of metal sits in a changing magnetic field (or moves through a non-uniform one), emfs are induced throughout its volume and circulate in closed loops. These are eddy currents.

By Lenz's law they oppose the change that causes them, so they produce a dragging force on a moving conductor and heat in a stationary one.

Effect of eddy currents Application
Retarding force on a conductor moving in a field electromagnetic braking of trains and balances
Heating of the metal induction furnace, induction cooker
Opposing rotation damping of galvanometer coils, speedometer
Energy loss in a core the problem that lamination solves

Lamination cuts the conducting path into thin sheets separated by insulation, so the eddy loops can only be small and the loss falls sharply.

Eddy-current loss grows as B^2f^2t^2 for sheet thickness t, which is why cores are made of thin sheets and why high-frequency cores use ferrite.

16.2 Self and mutual inductance; energy stored in an inductor

16.2.1 Self-inductance

A current in a coil produces flux through the coil itself. If the current changes, that flux changes and induces an emf in the same coil — self-induction. For a coil of N turns,

N\Phi=LI \qquad\text{and}\qquad \varepsilon=-L\frac{dI}{dt}

L is the self-inductance, measured in henry (H): 1 H = 1 Wb A⁻¹ = 1 V s A⁻¹. It depends only on the geometry of the coil and on the core material, not on the current.

For a long solenoid of N turns, area A, length l (with n=N/l),

L=\frac{\mu_0N^2A}{l}=\mu_0n^2Al

The N^2 is worth remembering: doubling the number of turns on the same former quadruples the inductance.

The back emf. When you close a switch on a coil, the current rises gradually, because the growing current induces an emf that opposes the growth.

When you open the switch, the current tries to fall quickly, the induced emf is large and in the direction that maintains the current — which is why a switch on an inductive circuit sparks, and why a fluorescent lamp needs a choke.

An inductor is the electrical analogue of mass: it resists any change in its current.

Element Resists change of Law
Resistor current (by dissipating energy) V=IR
Capacitor voltage Q=CV
Inductor current \varepsilon=-L\,dI/dt

16.2.2 Mutual inductance

Two coils close together are coupled: a changing current in coil 1 changes the flux through coil 2 and induces an emf there. For a flux linkage N_2\Phi_2 in the secondary,

N_2\Phi_2=MI_1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \varepsilon_2=-M\frac{dI_1}{dt}

M is the mutual inductance, also in henry. It depends on the geometry of both coils, their separation and orientation, and the core between them — but not on the current. For two coils of N_1 and N_2 turns wound on the same long solenoid of area A and length l,

M=\frac{\mu_0N_1N_2A}{l}

The reciprocity theorem states M_{12}=M_{21}: the emf in coil 2 per unit rate of change of current in coil 1 equals the emf in coil 1 for the same rate of change in coil 2. The transformer is the standard application.

Inductance is geometry, not current

L and M do not change when the current changes. What changes is the emf, which is proportional to dI/dt. A question that says "the current is doubled, so the inductance doubles" is wrong; doubling the current only doubles the stored energy and the flux.

16.2.3 Energy stored in an inductor

Building up a current in an inductor requires work against the back emf. The work done in raising the current from 0 to I is

U=\frac12LI^2

Energy stored in an inductor

Setting up. A coil of inductance L carries a current i that is rising. The back emf is \varepsilon=L\,di/dt (magnitude), so the source must supply power P=\varepsilon i.

Step 1 — power delivered against the back emf.

P=\varepsilon i=L\,i\frac{di}{dt}

Step 2 — power is the rate of change of stored energy.

\frac{dU}{dt}=L\,i\frac{di}{dt}

Step 3 — integrate from i=0 to i=I.

U=\int_0^I L\,i\,di=\frac12LI^2

Result. U=\frac12LI^2 joules.

What it means. The energy is stored in the magnetic field, not in the wire. For a long solenoid, dividing U by the volume Al and using B=\mu_0nI gives the energy density

u=\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}

so every cubic metre of a 1 T field holds about 4\times10^{5} J.

Worked example 16.4 — inductance and stored energy

Problem. A solenoid 0.40 m long has 800 turns of area 5.0\times10^{-4} m². Find its self-inductance and the energy stored when it carries 3.0 A.

Solution. L=\dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(800)^2(5.0\times10^{-4})}{0.40} =1.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{H}.

U=\frac12LI^2=\frac12(1.0\times10^{-3})(3.0)^2=4.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{J}.

The inductance is about a millihenry — typical of a laboratory coil, and a reminder that 1 H is a large unit.

16.3 Peak and rms values; impedance, phase, power and Q-factor of LCR circuits

16.3.1 Peak, mean and rms values

An alternating current reverses direction periodically. Write it as

i=i_0\sin\omega t

Value Symbol Expression For i_0=1 A
Peak (maximum) i_0 — 1.000 A
Mean over a full cycle \bar i 0 0
Mean over a half cycle \bar i 2i_0/\pi 0.637 A
Root mean square i_{rms} i_0/\sqrt{2} 0.707 A

The full-cycle mean is zero because the positive and negative halves cancel, so a moving-coil meter (which responds to the mean) reads zero on AC.

The rms value is the value of the direct current that would produce the same heating in a resistor, and it is what AC meters and the 220 V mains rating mean.

I_{rms}=\frac{i_0}{\sqrt{2}}=0.707\,i_0, \qquad V_{rms}=\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}

The form factor is I_{rms}/\bar I=0.707/0.637=1.11 for a sine wave.

rms and peak in power

The power is P=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi, not V_0I_0\cos\phi. Using peak values gives an answer twice too large. Equivalently P=\frac12V_0I_0\cos\phi — the factor \frac12 and the two 1/\sqrt{2} factors are the same statement.

16.3.2 Resistance, reactance and impedance

Circuit element Opposition Symbol Phase of current relative to voltage
Resistor R resistance R R in phase
Inductor L inductive reactance X_L=\omega L lags by 90°
Capacitor C capacitive reactance X_C=1/\omega C leads by 90°

X_L rises with frequency (a rapid change is harder to establish in a coil); X_C falls with frequency (a capacitor passes rapid changes more easily). At very high frequency an inductor is nearly an open circuit and a capacitor nearly a short circuit.

Series LCR circuit. The same current flows through all three, so the voltages are V_R=IR, V_L=IX_L, V_C=IX_C. The voltages across L and C are 180° out of phase and partly cancel. Adding them as phasors gives the supply voltage

V=\sqrt{V_R^2+(V_L-V_C)^2}=I\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}

so the impedance is

Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \tan\phi=\frac{X_L-X_C}{R}

where \phi is the phase angle by which the voltage leads the current. If X_L>X_C, \phi>0 and the circuit is inductive (current lags). If X_C>X_L, the circuit is capacitive (current leads).

Worked example 16.5 — impedance and phase

Problem. A series circuit has R=30\ \Omega, X_L=70\ \Omega and X_C=30\ \Omega, connected to a 200 V (rms) supply. Find Z, the current and the phase angle.

Solution. X_L-X_C=40\ \Omega, so Z=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=50\ \Omega.

I_{rms}=V_{rms}/Z=200/50=4.0\ \text{A}.

\tan\phi=40/30=1.33, so \phi=53^{\circ} with the voltage leading — an inductive circuit, current lagging.

16.3.3 Resonance

As the frequency of the supply is varied, X_L rises and X_C falls. At one frequency they are equal and cancel exactly:

X_L=X_C \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \omega_0L=\frac{1}{\omega_0C} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \omega_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}

f_0=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}

At resonance:

  • Z=R, the minimum possible impedance;
  • I=V/R, the maximum current;
  • \phi=0, so the current and voltage are in phase and the power factor is 1;
  • V_L and V_C are equal in magnitude and opposite in phase, so they cancel in the supply voltage — but each can be much larger than the supply voltage.

That last point is the useful and dangerous one. Since V_L=IX_L and I=V/R,

\frac{V_L}{V}=\frac{X_L}{R}=\frac{\omega_0L}{R}=Q

the quality factor. A circuit with Q=100 develops 100 times the supply voltage across the capacitor — the principle of radio tuning, and the reason a resonant circuit can destroy itself.

Q=\frac{\omega_0L}{R}=\frac{1}{\omega_0CR}=\frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}, \qquad Q=\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}

where \Delta f is the bandwidth, the width of the resonance curve at I=I_{max}/\sqrt{2}. A high Q means a tall, narrow peak: the circuit responds strongly to one frequency and hardly at all to its neighbours.

At resonance Value
Impedance Z=R (minimum)
Current I=V/R (maximum)
Phase angle 0
Power factor 1
V_L and V_C equal, opposite, each Q times the supply
Frequency f_0=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})
Resonance means maximum current, not zero voltage

At resonance the total reactance is zero, so the impedance is smallest and the current largest. Distractors offer "impedance maximum" or "current zero". Also, the voltage across the capacitor is not zero — it is Q times the supply voltage.

Worked example 16.6 — resonance and Q

Problem. A series LCR circuit has L=1.0 mH, C=1.0\ \muF and R=10\ \Omega. Find the resonant frequency, the Q-factor and the bandwidth.

Solution. f_0=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} =\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{(1.0\times10^{-3})(1.0\times10^{-6})}} =\dfrac{1}{2\pi(3.16\times10^{-5})}=5.0\times10^{3}\ \text{Hz}.

Q=\dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}}=\dfrac{1}{10}\sqrt{\dfrac{10^{-3}}{10^{-6}}} =\dfrac{1}{10}(31.6)=3.2.

\Delta f=f_0/Q=5000/3.2=1.6\times10^{3}\ \text{Hz} — a broad, low-Q resonance.

16.3.4 Power in an AC circuit

The instantaneous power p=vi rises and falls, and can even be negative for part of the cycle (energy returned to the supply by a capacitor or inductor). The average power over a cycle is

P=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi

where \cos\phi=R/Z is the power factor.

Circuit \phi \cos\phi Average power
Pure R 0 1 V_{rms}I_{rms}
Pure L 90° 0 0
Pure C 90° 0 0
Series LCR between R/Z I_{rms}^2R

In a purely reactive circuit the current is wattless: it flows, the ammeter reads it, but no net energy is consumed — the energy shuttles back and forth between the source and the field.

The wattless component of a general current is I_{rms}\sin\phi, and the active (power-carrying) component is I_{rms}\cos\phi.

Note also that P=I_{rms}^2R always, whatever the reactances: only the resistance dissipates energy.

Worked example 16.7 — power and power factor

Problem. An AC circuit draws 2.0 A (rms) at 220 V (rms) with a phase angle of 60°. Find the power, the power factor and the wattless current.

Solution. P=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi=(220)(2.0)(0.50)=220\ \text{W}.

Power factor \cos60^{\circ}=0.50.

Wattless current =I_{rms}\sin60^{\circ}=2.0(0.866)=1.7\ \text{A}.

The other 1.0 A is the active component, and 220\times1.0=220 W ✓.

16.4 Rectification with a diode bridge

16.4.1 The diode as a one-way valve

A p–n junction diode conducts when it is forward biased (p side positive) and blocks when it is reverse biased.

In the forward direction a small voltage (about 0.7 V for silicon) is needed before the current rises steeply; in reverse only a tiny leakage current flows until breakdown.

Rectification is the conversion of AC into a unidirectional (pulsating DC) current using this one-way property.

16.4.2 Half-wave rectification

One diode in series with the load passes current only during the half cycle in which it is forward biased. The output is a series of pulses with gaps:

Quantity Half-wave
Diodes 1
Output pulses per input cycle 1
Ripple frequency f (50 Hz for 50 Hz mains)
Mean (DC) output V_0/\pi=0.318V_0
rms output V_0/2
Ripple factor 1.21
Efficiency about 40.6 %

16.4.3 The full-wave bridge rectifier

Four diodes in a bridge pass current through the load in the same direction on both half cycles. On the positive half, diodes D1 and D3 conduct; on the negative half, D2 and D4 conduct. The load therefore sees a pulse for every half cycle.

Quantity Half-wave Full-wave bridge
Diodes 1 4
Pulses per cycle 1 2
Ripple frequency f 2f
Mean output 0.318V_0 0.637V_0
rms output 0.500V_0 0.707V_0
Ripple factor 1.21 0.48
Efficiency 40.6 % 81.2 %
Peak inverse voltage per diode V_0 V_0

The bridge is better on every count except that it uses four diodes and two of them are always in series with the load, so the output is lower than the peak by about 1.4 V.

Smoothing. A large capacitor across the load charges to the peak and discharges slowly through the load between peaks, filling the gaps. The residual variation is the ripple, and it falls as C and as the load resistance rise.

A regulator stage after the capacitor gives a steady DC.

What a rectifier does not do

A rectifier produces pulsating DC, not a steady battery voltage, and it does not change the power available. The output frequency of the ripple is twice the input frequency for a full-wave rectifier — a very common question.

And a diode is not a resistor: its forward resistance is small but not zero, and it drops about 0.7 V.

Worked example 16.8 — rectifier output

Problem. A bridge rectifier is fed with 50 Hz AC whose peak voltage is 12 V. Find the ripple frequency and the mean output voltage (ignore the diode drops).

Solution. Ripple frequency =2f=100\ \text{Hz}.

Mean output =\dfrac{2V_0}{\pi}=\dfrac{2(12)}{\pi}=7.6\ \text{V}.

The rms output would be V_0/\sqrt{2}=8.5 V; the mean is lower because the waveform is not sinusoidal.

Mutual inductance N_2\Phi_2=MI_1; \varepsilon_2=-M\,dI_1/dt; M=\mu_0N_1N_2A/l; M_{12}=M_{21}

Reactance X_L=\omega L (current lags 90°); X_C=1/\omega C (current leads 90°)

Chapter summary

  • The flux through a coil is \Phi=BA\cos\theta; the emf is the negative rate of change of flux linkage, \varepsilon=-N\,d\Phi/dt, and only a changing flux induces one.
  • Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change in flux; that opposition is what makes the law a statement of energy conservation.
  • A rod moving across a field has \varepsilon=Bvl; the magnetic drag is B^2l^2v/R and the mechanical power you supply equals the I^2R heat produced.
  • A coil rotating in a field gives \varepsilon=NBA\omega\sin\omega t; the peak emf is NBA\omega and it occurs when the flux through the coil is zero.
  • A transformer obeys V_s/V_p=N_s/N_p=I_p/I_s; it needs alternating current, cannot change the frequency, and loses energy to copper, eddy currents, hysteresis and leakage.
  • Self-inductance is N\Phi=LI with \varepsilon=-L\,dI/dt; a solenoid has L=\mu_0N^2A/l, and the stored energy is \frac12LI^2, in the field with density B^2/2\mu_0.
  • Mutual inductance M couples two coils and is the basis of the transformer; M_{12}=M_{21}.
  • rms values are peak values divided by \sqrt{2}; the power is V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi, never V_0I_0\cos\phi.
  • In series LCR, Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}; at resonance X_L=X_C, Z=R, the current is maximum and the voltages across L and C are Q times the supply.
  • A bridge rectifier uses four diodes, conducts on both half cycles, gives a mean output 2V_0/\pi and a ripple at twice the supply frequency.

  1. State Faraday's and Lenz's laws, derive the motional emf and explain self- and mutual inductance with the energy stored in an inductor. [10]
  2. Analyse a series LCR circuit with an AC source: impedance, resonance and power factor. Describe the transformer. [10]

Model answer D1: electromagnetic induction and inductance (10 marks)

Introduction. Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an emf is induced in it. Magnetic flux is \Phi = BA\cos\theta, in weber.

Laws.

  1. Faraday's law: the induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage, \varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}.
  2. Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change that produces it. The minus sign expresses this, and it is a statement of conservation of energy: if the current helped the change, energy would be created from nothing.

Motional emf. A rod of length l moves at speed v perpendicular to a field B on rails. The area changes at the rate lv, so \varepsilon = Blv. The current is I = Blv/R, the force opposing the motion is F = B^2l^2v/R and the power supplied is Fv = \varepsilon^2/R.

Inductance.

Quantity Definition Formula
Self-inductance L flux linkage per unit current \varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}, solenoid L = \mu_0n^2Al
Mutual inductance M flux in coil 2 per unit current in coil 1 \varepsilon_2 = -M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}
Energy in an inductor work to build up current U = \tfrac12LI^2

The unit of L and M is the henry. Energy density of a magnetic field is \dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0}.

Other effects. Eddy currents are induced in solid conductors, giving electromagnetic braking and induction heating, but also wasting energy in transformer cores (reduced by lamination). A DC generator has a commutator, an AC generator slip rings.

Numerical. A rod 0.5\ \text{m} long moves at 4\ \text{m s}^{-1} in B = 0.2\ \text{T}: \varepsilon = 0.2\times0.5\times4 = 0.4\ \text{V}.

In a circuit of 2\ \Omega the current is 0.2\ \text{A}, the retarding force 0.2\times0.5\times0.2 = 0.02\ \text{N} and the power 0.08\ \text{W} (equal to Fv = 0.02\times4).

A solenoid with L = 0.5\ \text{H} carrying 4\ \text{A} stores \tfrac12(0.5)(16) = 4\ \text{J}.

Conclusion. The induced emf is the rate of change of flux, and its direction (Lenz) ensures energy conservation.

Model answer D2: AC circuits and the transformer (10 marks)

Introduction. For an AC source V = V_0\sin\omega t: V_{rms} = V_0/\sqrt2. A resistor has V and I in phase. In an inductor, V leads I by 90^{\circ} with reactance X_L = \omega L. In a capacitor, V lags I by 90^{\circ} with reactance X_C = 1/\omega C.

Series LCR circuit. The impedance is Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, the current is I = V/Z and the phase angle is \tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}.

Resonance. When X_L = X_C, Z = R is minimum and the current is maximum. The resonant frequency is f_0 = \dfrac1{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}. The sharpness is given by the quality factor Q = \dfrac{\omega_0L}{R}. Radio tuning uses this.

Power. The average power is P = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi, where \cos\phi = R/Z is the power factor. In a pure inductor or capacitor P = 0, and the current is called wattless.

Transformer. It works on mutual induction. For an ideal transformer, \dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{I_p}{I_s}. A step-up transformer has N_s > N_p. Efficiency is \dfrac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}.

Losses are copper loss (I^2R), eddy current loss, hysteresis loss, flux leakage and humming; they are reduced by thick wire, laminated cores, soft iron and a good winding.

Power is transmitted at high voltage so that I^2R loss in the lines is low.

Circuit Phase of current Power
R only in phase VI
L only lags 90^{\circ} 0
C only leads 90^{\circ} 0
LCR at resonance in phase VI (maximum)

Numerical. R = 30\ \Omega, L = 0.2\ \text{H}, C = 100\ \mu\text{F}, 220\ \text{V}, 50\ \text{Hz}: X_L = 62.8\ \Omega, X_C = 31.8\ \Omega, so Z = \sqrt{30^2 + 31^2} = 43.1\ \Omega, I = 5.1\ \text{A}, \cos\phi = 0.70 and P = I^2R = 780\ \text{W}.

The resonant frequency is f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{0.2\times10^{-4}}) = 35.6\ \text{Hz}. A transformer stepping 220\ \text{V} down to 11\ \text{V} has a turns ratio 20:1.

Conclusion. Current in an LCR circuit is greatest at resonance, and only the resistance consumes average power.
